messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 77

He grew up in a small city in Vietnam, the second son of a seamstress and a fisherman. By the time he was six, his mother noticed he could not stop moving—spinning in the courtyard, mimicking the dancers on the television her employer had given her. She enrolled him in a traditional dance class when he was eight. At eighteen he moved to Hanoi to join a contemporary dance company. He met his wife there, a lighting technician. They married when he was twenty-seven.

When he was thirty-six, his wife’s younger brother, a volunteer with an international medical organization, was killed by a mortar in a conflict zone in the Middle East. The family grieved. He felt an overwhelming pull to go in his brother-in-law’s place. He told his wife it was the only thing that made sense. She did not argue. She understood grief in her own way. He spent the next eight months driving supply trucks across contested roads, carrying food and medicine to clinics in bombed-out neighborhoods. At first the danger felt abstract. Then one afternoon an ambulance in front of him hit an improvised explosive device. He saw the driver’s body through the smoke. He kept driving. After that he began to feel the fear in his chest, a tightness that did not leave.

His body remembers before his mind does. In session he describes the sound of shelling in the distance that became so familiar he stopped flinching, but now any sudden loud noise—a door slamming in the theater, a dropped metal tray—sends his shoulders up to his ears. His heart pounds for minutes afterward. He avoids watching news footage of any war. He cannot eat in restaurants with outdoor seating because he needs to see all exits. He shakes his head when I ask about nightmares. Then he tells me he wakes at three in the morning, drenched in sweat, certain he is back in the supply truck. He rarely tells his wife what he sees in the dreams. He does not want her to worry.

The hardest part is the dancing. Before he left, he moved with a fluency that made audience members cry. He could improvise for an hour and feel no fatigue. Now his body feels foreign, heavy, as if every joint is locked. He goes to rehearsal every day, but he avoids the pieces that require sudden turns or physical contact with other dancers. A partner’s hand on his back makes him stiffen. He has started arriving early to practice alone, repeating the same simple sequence of steps, trying to coax the old ease back. It does not come. He tells me he feels like a puppet whose strings are tangled. He used to believe dance was a form of prayer. Now he is not sure it is anything.

His wife has stopped asking him to perform at home. She watches him from the doorway of their bedroom, then turns away. He knows she is hurt. He wants to reach for her, but his hands hang at his sides. He feels hollow. He scored 77 on the PTSD checklist. He does not ask what the number means. He only says, “I used to know what my body was for.”
